Q: How should I continue learning Java programming? A:

If you want to make a step forward, this is what you should learn:

  1. Data structures and algorithms, there are various sites out there that have useful exercises to solidify the knowledge and most of them support many languages including Java. It is very important to have those basics down. I think you will learn big O along the way, because this is decisive for both algorithms and data structures (i.e. the operations on them).

  2. IDE. Get familiar with an IDE (IntelliJ or Eclipse) and learn how to use a debugger. Sooner or later you will spend time looking for bugs and System.out.println() is not the most efficient debugging tool, or is useless if you have to do remote debugging. Refactoring is also very useful and both mentioned IDEs have tools for that. If you look at your code after some years you will be thankful if you left a brief description of what a class or method does (although it should be obvious from the name), so learn Javadoc too and as bonus learn how to write readme files in markdown (SO is using markdown, you should already know that). Learn dependency management (maven or gradle) and how to resolve conflicts. Finally learn how to use a versioning control system e.g. git.

  3. Spring Boot is the next step to a full stack programmer. Swing and AWT is rarely used today, the frontends are often web-based: thymeleaf templates (modern JSP) and controllers (spring-boot-starter-web). Often data needs to be stored, so Jakarte Persistence (spring-boot-starter-data-jpa) would be next. Then you want to have a configuration and not hardcode everything, so learn how to use .yaml or .properties files and how to inject their values. JSON serialization and deserialization is often important, e.g. to support custom date formats, so learn Jackson (or Gson, but it is less powerful). If you are familiar with most spring boot packages and still want to learn more, then I would recommend to look into docker.

Q: How to avoid certain formatting with PAR? A:

It seems that you are missing the `PARINIT` environment variable, which should be configured to define standard text characters that belong to a body (not suffix/prefix) e.g., `_a_A.,!?`. Try running your command with the additional argument `B=_a_A.,!?`.

Q: How to calculate the mean value of a variable on a specific day of the year over several years A:

You can group by multiple dimensions by giving a list of dimensions.

da.groupby(['valid_time.month', 'valid_time.day']).mean()

Q: How can I implement a single-instance Java application? A:

We use file locking for this (grab an exclusive lock on a magic file in the user's app data directory), but we are primarily interested in preventing multiple instances from ever running.

If you are trying to have the second instance pass command line arguments, etc... to the first instance, then using a socket connection on localhost will be killing two birds with one stone. General algorithm:

  • On launch, try to open a listener on port XXXX on localhost
  • if it fails, open a writer to that port on localhost and send the command line arguments, and then shutdown
  • otherwise, listen on port XXXXX on localhost. When receiving the command line arguments, process them as if the app was launched with that command line.
